column3: Close to the Greek.
Close to the Greek.
The Greek says things “came into being,” rather than explicitly “were made.”
Close to the Greek.
καταλαμβάνω can mean grasp or seize; BSB selects “overcome.”

Close to the Greek.
“He came” supplies the missing main predicate before the Greek purpose clause.
BSB attaches “coming into the world” to the Light; the Greek participle can also attach grammatically to “every man.”
The Greek coordinates the clauses with “and,” rather than making the world’s creation concessive with “though.”
Close to the Greek.
BSB moves the phrase about believing before the granting of authority.
The Greek separately names the will of flesh and the will of a man; BSB compresses these as “the desire or will of man” and supplies “children.”
The Greek uses the image of dwelling in a tent; “Son” is not explicit after “only-begotten.”
The Greek uses present “testifies” and past “This was,” rather than “testified” and “This is.”
BSB leaves the critical text’s “for” (ὅτι) untranslated and renders grace “upon” grace.
Close to the Greek.
The critical text directly calls Him “only-begotten God”; BSB expresses this as “Son, who is Himself God” and renders “bosom” as “side.”
The Greek says Jews sent priests from Jerusalem, rather than explicitly identifying them as “Jews of Jerusalem.”
The Greek repeats “confessed” around “did not deny”; BSB recasts this as not refusing to confess and openly declaring.
“Then who are you?” expands the Greek “What then?”

BSB leaves the clause unfinished into verse 25; the Greek has the finite “were” here.
